title: How can you learn to speak more clearly in a case interview?
description: The interviewer needs to follow your reasoning. Calm, understandable explanations are more valuable than impressive-sounding language.
hook: You learn to speak more clearly in a case by practising four habits every day: answer first, keep sentences short, pause between ideas, and give every number a unit and a meaning. You do not need to sound like a consultant to pass a case; you need to be easy to follow. Five to ten minutes of the exercises below, most days, makes a real difference within a couple of weeks.
body:
What clear sounds like

The interviewer has to follow your reasoning in real time, without seeing your notes. Calm, plain explanations are worth more than impressive vocabulary. A clear spoken thought in a case usually has three parts: the equation, the result and the meaning.

Revenue is 10,000 orders times $40 per order, so $400,000. Orders haven't changed, so any fall in revenue has to come from order value.

That is a complete thought. Compare it with "So it's 10,000 times 40, which is, um, 400,000, and orders are the same, and the value, I guess, could be lower." Same maths, but the listener has to do the work of finding your point.

The same principle scales up. At the start of any answer, say where you are going ("Two reasons"); at the end, say what it means. The pyramid principle explains why answer-first is easier to follow.

Three exercises for 5 to 10 minutes a day

1. Warm up your speech

Spend two or three minutes loosening up: relax your jaw, try a couple of tongue twisters slowly and then at speed, and read a few business sentences aloud. A free guided routine such as Speech On (speechon.app) makes this easy. Warm-ups help you feel ready to speak, but they do not replace practising case explanations, so treat them as preparation, not the main event.

2. Give a 60-second recommendation

Pick any business decision, from a news story or a case you have done, and deliver a recommendation in a fixed shape: the answer, two reasons, one risk and a next step. Record it. Here is an illustrative one:

The client should launch the premium tier. Two reasons. First, 15% of its 40,000 customers say they would pay $10 a month more; that's 6,000 customers and about $720k a year. Second, it costs $300k to build, so it pays back in about five months. The main risk is cannibalisation: some of those customers may already buy add-ons that the premium tier would replace. Next step: test it with 1,000 customers before a full launch.

Check the numbers: 15% × 40,000 = 6,000 customers; 6,000 × $10 × 12 months = $720k; $300k ÷ $720k × 12 months = 5 months. Every number has a unit and every number has a job in the argument.

3. Replace rush with pauses

Say a sentence, stop for a beat, and continue. Pause especially between a calculation and its implication, and before your headline. It is fine to take thinking time. A short silence sounds confident; a rushed sentence that changes direction halfway sounds unsure.

Record yourself and listen for three things

Record one explanation a day and play it back. Listen for:

  • Sentences that change direction halfway. Usually a sign you started talking before you knew your point. Pause, decide the headline, then speak.
  • Claims with no support. "Costs are the problem" needs a number or a reason after it.
  • Numbers without units. "Seven point six" could be anything. Say "7.6% of revenue" or "$7.6M".

Then record it again, fixing only the biggest issue. One improvement a day adds up faster than trying to fix everything at once.

Weak versus strong, side by side

Weak:

I looked at the chart and there's a lot going on, but basically the north region seems kind of lower, and maybe it's the competitor, or prices, and I think we should probably look at that.

Strong:

The north region is the problem. Its sales fell 20% while the other regions grew. I'd like to check whether that's one large customer or a broad decline.

The strong version is shorter, leads with the point, quantifies it and proposes a next step. It is also no more formal. Clarity is not a performed executive voice or a particular accent; it is order and brevity.

Common mistakes

  • Narrating your working. Saying every step as you think it. Think briefly in silence, then give the organised version.
  • Hedging every sentence. "I think maybe possibly" weakens a good point. State it, then say how confident you are once.
  • Long sentences joined with "and". Break them into two or three short ones.
  • Speeding up on numbers. Numbers are where the interviewer most needs to hear you. Slow down for them.

Try it now

1. Rewrite this answer-first: "We looked at volume, which is flat, then price, which is down 8%, so the revenue drop is from price."

Show the answer

"The revenue drop comes from price, which is down 8%. Volume is flat. Next, I'd like to see whether we cut prices or whether our mix shifted to cheaper products."

2. Say this calculation in the three-part shape: 2,000 customers each paying $50 a month.

Show the answer

"Revenue is 2,000 customers times $50, so $100,000 a month, or $1.2M a year. That gives us the baseline to test the price change against." Equation, result, meaning.

3. Give a 60-second recommendation on whether a coffee chain should open on Sundays. Record it and check: answer first, two reasons, one risk, one next step.

Show the answer

A strong version opens with a clear yes or no, gives two reasons with a number each (for example, expected Sunday sales against extra staff cost), names one risk such as staff availability, and ends with a test, such as a six-week trial in five stores. If you ran over 60 seconds, cut detail from the reasons, not the structure.

Where to practise next

Use the routines on the interview skills page, and read how to come across as clear and calm for the wider picture. To polish the end of a case, see the 60-second recommendation, and rehearse the phrases for each stage with perfect casing.
